The space — asks, changes, units

The space is the one surface between you and the machine. It renders in the sidebar (the Tandem icon), and each thinking space you open (Tandem: Open the Space) gets its own editor tab, titled with that space’s name — the name you gave it when you named it, or, when you never named it, its slug read back as plain words ("docs-duty-and-tabs" becomes "Docs duty and tabs"). Opening a second thinking space opens a second tab and leaves the first one open — several thinking spaces stay open at the same time. Every tab shows the same live state for the space it was opened for.

When no space can be named — nothing is chosen and nothing is recorded — no tab opens. You are told why, in one plain sentence, instead.

What derivation does with an ask

Behind one captured ask runs a pipeline of rounds, each fail-soft:

  1. Contextualize — one bounded, cited reading of the repository, persisted per ask, so later rounds build on an established reading.

  2. Ground — the ask becomes changes: sentences with real landing files and acceptance criteria. Line numbers are refused by design — anchors are structural (file, symbol), so they survive edits.

  3. Gap-close — a judge with exactly two outcomes: the set covers the ask, or here are the missing changes, concrete and grounded.

  4. Impact — the adjacent code that must move too (callers, configuration, documentation).

  5. Intent coverage — every clause of your ask must be served by some change; an unserved clause comes back as a question with a recommendation, never silence.

  6. Assessment — vague acceptance criteria are rewritten to observable ones (closed verdicts: observable / vague / untestable).

  7. Challenger — contradictions between the changes and your decisions in force are raised as questions. It never changes anything.

Units and pins

Changes cluster into units by real code coupling (same file is decisive). The clustering is code, not a model — and your pins outrank it: Merge into one slice forces a union; Split out severs a pair.

Staleness and re-grounding

Every grounded change carries a fingerprint of the repository state it was true for. When the code moves underneath, the change is marked stale; press the stale badge to re-ground. A signed TEP whose content drifted refuses dispatch until re-signed.

Panic

The Panic button (behind a confirm) clears everything derived — changes, units, open questions, unsigned cuts — and keeps what is yours: your asks and your settled decisions. It is refused once any TEP was signed in the space.
